Rottenness
rŏt´ĕn-nĕs
n. (decay from within, especially of the bones; Hebrew raqab)
From rotten, Old Norse rotinn, decayed. Scripture places the decay in the bones — the innermost and strongest part of the frame — where it cannot be seen and cannot be reached.

Biblical Definition

Rottenness in Scripture is almost always internal and almost always in the bones. Solomon uses it twice in the Proverbs, and both times the outward frame is intact while the core gives way. “A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones” (Pro 12:4). And on the passion that eats a man alive: “A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones” (Pro 14:30). Isaiah turns it on a nation that had every appearance of health: “so their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the LORD of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel” (Isa 5:24). Hosea makes the LORD Himself the agent: “Therefore will I be unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as rottenness” (Hos 5:12). And Habakkuk, hearing what is coming upon his people, feels it in his own frame: “rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble” (Hab 3:16). The picture is consistent: what destroys does not always arrive from outside.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines rottenness as a state of being decayed; putrefaction; unsoundness; and figuratively, moral corruption within.

expand to see more

ROTTENNESS, n. State of being rotten; putrefaction; decay; unsoundness.

ROTTEN, a. Putrid; carious; decomposed by the natural process of decay.

2. Not firm or trusty; unsound; defective in principle; as a rotten heart.

Key Scripture

Pro 12:4 — "A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones."

Pro 14:30 — "A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones."

Isa 5:24 — "Therefore as the fire devoureth the stubble, and the flame consumeth the chaff, so their root shall be as rottenness, and their blossom shall go up as dust: because they have cast away the law of the LORD of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel."

Hos 5:12 — "Therefore will I be unto Ephraim as a moth, and to the house of Judah as rottenness."

Modern Corruption

Envy is treated as a harmless private feeling, while Proverbs classes it with a disease of the bones.

expand to see more

Proverbs 14:30 sets two conditions side by side: a sound heart is the life of the flesh, but envy the rottenness of the bones. Modern moral vocabulary has almost no category for envy. It is not litigable, it harms no one visibly, and it can be carried a whole life without confession. Scripture treats it as a wasting disease of the skeleton — the part of a man that holds him up. That is not hyperbole in a book that also says a merry heart doeth good like a medicine.

Hosea 5:12 supplies the fearful half of the doctrine. The LORD says He will be to Judah as rottenness — not as a sword, not as an invading army, but as slow decay. Judgment does not always come as an event. Sometimes it comes as a nation quietly losing the strength it assumes it still has, and the prophets name that as the LORD's own work, not as historical misfortune.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew raqab (H7538), rottenness, decay of bone or wood; maq (H4716), rot; the figure is fixed to 'etsem, bone, the frame's inmost strength.

expand to see more

Hebrew raqab (H7538) — rottenness; Proverbs 12:4, 14:30, Hosea 5:12.

Hebrew 'etsem (H6106) — bone; the seat of the decay in every proverb.

Hebrew maq (H4716) — rot, decay; Isaiah 5:24, the root as rottenness.

Hebrew qin'ah (H7068) — envy, jealousy; the cause named in Proverbs 14:30.

Hebrew 'ash (H6211) — moth; paired with rottenness in Hosea 5:12.

Usage

"“Envy the rottenness of the bones” — a private sin classed as skeletal disease."

"“Their root shall be as rottenness” — the blossom still showing."

"“Therefore will I be unto Ephraim as a moth” — judgment that arrives slowly."
